Definition: The uncertainty of ±1 in the last digit of a measurement. If this uncertainty is different from ±1, it is written as part of the number; for example, 23.45 ± 0.05 indicates an uncertainty of ±5 in the last digit.
The lowest possible temperature, 0.0 K or -273.16 °C.
A measure of the amount of light absorbed by a chemical.
A constant the value of which depends on the sample and the wavelength at which the measurement is made in spectroscopy.
The degree of closeness between a measured value and the true value.
Any substance that donates protons, or as Lewis acids are electron-pair acceptors.
The oxide of a nonmetal that forms an acid when dissolved in water.
The value of the equilibrium expression for the dissociation of a weak acid.
The structures of colliding molecules at the moment of collision, generally thought to be intermediate between the structures of the products and of the reactants.
The increase in potential energy, due to a molecular collision, necessary to convert a reactant into a product.

A listing of elemental substances in the order of their ability to be oxidized or reduced. This listing makes it possible to predict whether an element will cause the oxidation or the reduction of an ion of another element.
The reaction in which a double bond opens to form two additional single bonds.
The attractive force between two dissimilar substances.
An organic compound with an -OH group.
An organic compound with a terminal -CHO group.
The extremely reactive elements in the first group (column) of the periodic table. They all have ns1 electrons as valence electrons.
The very reactive elements in the second group (column) of the periodic table. They all have ns2 electrons as valence electrons.
Organic compounds with the general formula CnH2n+2.
Organic compounds with double bonds in their structures.
A functional group that is alkane in nature.
Organic compounds with triple bonds in their structures.
One or more distinct forms of an element; classification as an allotope is based on structure and physical properties. For example, diamond and graphite are two allotropes of carbon.
A helium nucleus.
Compounds, related to ammonia, in which one or more of the hydrogen atoms in ammonia have been replaced by organic functional groups.
An organic acid that contains both an amine and an acid functional group on adjacent carbon atoms.
A term meaning “without structure.”
A term describing a substance that can donate a proton and accept a proton.
A term describing a substance that can act as an acid or as a base.
The oxide of a metal or nonmetal that reacts with water to form an acid or a base, respectively.
An ion with a negative charge.
A term designating a system that involves water or a chemical mixture or solution having water as the solvent.
The equation that relates temperature to rate constant. K = Ae-Ea/RT.
The theory that an acid increases hydrogen ion concentration when dissolved and that a base increases hydroxide ion concentration when dissolved.
A functional group that is aromatic in nature.
A fundamental particle of chemistry. At present, 109 atoms are known and are arranged in an orderly manner in the periodic table.
The relative mass of an element as compared to the mass of the isotope C-12, which is defined as exactly 12.
The number of an element in the periodic table; also, a number representing the number of protons in the nucleus of an atom.
The orbital structure of an element; also, an orbital within an element.
A one- or two-letter abbreviation of an element's name. Some symbols (e.g., Pb for lead) are derived from Latin names of the elements.
Attractions between particles with partial or full charges. Forces described by Coulomb's law, hydrogen bonding, dipole- dipole attractions, and instantaneous dipole attractions.
The value of the equilibrium expression for the dissociation of water into H+ and OH−.
A quantity equal to 6.02 × 1023.
A statement of the direct relationship between the moles of a gas and the volume of that gas.

A term used to describe the position of an atom in a covalent molecule of the AX5 or AX6 basic structure. The axial atoms are on the vertical axis of the molecule in positions similar to the Earth's North and South Poles.

The quantum number that specifies the sublevel in which an electron is located; l may be any number from zero up to n - 1. When l is written as its letter equivalent, it represents an orbital where l = 0 = s; l = 1 = p; l = 2 = d; l = 3 = f.
A chemical equation that has the smallest whole-number coefficients for the reactants and products so that there is the same number of atoms of each element on both sides of the arrow.
A closed-end manometer used for measuring atmospheric pressure.
Any compound that increases the hydroxide concentration of a solution or is a proton acceptor. Lewis bases are electron-pair donors.
The oxide of a metal that forms a base when dissolved in water.
The value of the equilibrium expression for the dissociation of a weak base.
One of five basic geometrics-linear, trigonal planar, tetra­ hedral, trigonal planar, or octahedral-that a molecule may take.
A galvanic cell used to produce electricity for consumer items such as flashlights, portable radios, and heart pacemakers.

The statements that the absorbance of a sample is the product of the absorptivity, optical path length, and sample concentration; A = abc or (A) = εbc. (a is the absorptivity and ε is the molar absorptivity.).
An electron.
A Lewis base that donates two pairs of electrons.
An acid that contains hydrogen and one other element in its formula.
A cubic structure in which one atom is at each of the eight corners and one atom is in the center of the unit cell.
The model of the atom developed by Niels Bohr. This model views electrons as circling the nucleus like a miniature solar system.
The temperature at which the vapor pressure of a liquid is equal to 760 millimeters of mercury (1.00 atmospheres); also, the temperature at which a gas condenses. Also called condensation point.
The temperature increase of the boiling point per molal of solute particles.
The average number of bonds per atom covalently bonded to a central atom.
A pair of electrons that participate in a covalent bond.
The law that expresses the inverse relationship between the volume and the pressure of a gas; PV = constant.
The equation that relates the atomic dimensions in a crystal to the angles at which monochromatic X rays will undergo constructive reinforcement.
The theory that acids are proton donors and bases are proton acceptors.
The allotrope of carbon that has the formula C60.
The moles of strong acid or strong base required to change the pH of a liter of buffer by l pH unit.
An aqueous solution containing a conjugate acid and its conjugate base in a molar ratio greater than 0.1 and less than 10.0.
The violent boiling that occurs when a solution becomes superheated.
A tube approximately 1 centimeter in diameter that is used for measuring liquid volumes of 10-100 milliliters.
An instrument used to determine heat energy.
A substance that speeds up the rate of a chemical reaction by providing an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy.
An ion with a positive charge.
The voltage of a galvanic cell under nonstandard state conditions.
The process of separating a solid from a liquid by spinning it rapidly to artificially increase the gravitational force.
A nuclear reaction that produces more neutrons than were needed to initiate it, therefore causing more reactions than occurred in the preceding step.
The law that expresses the direct relationship between the temperature and volume of a gas: P/V = constant.
A Lewis base that usually has more than one pair of electrons to donate.
An isomer with substituents on the same side of the double bond.
A system in which mass cannot be lost to or gained from the surroundings.

A number placed in front of a chemical formula to represent the number of molecules of that substance that are included in the equation. This number multiplies the number of atoms in the formula unit.
The sum of all the attractive forces in a pure substance.
Any one of several physical properties of a solution that change depending on the amount of solute particles present in the solution.
The theory of kinetics, which relates reaction rates to the frequency, energy, and orientation of molecules in collisions.
A combination of one or more compounds or anions with a metal ion by coordinate covalent bonding. Also called a complex.
A reaction between a Lewis acid and a Lewis base.
A combination of two or more elements into a distinct substance with definite physical properties.
A qualitative term indicating a large amount of solute in a given amount of solvent.
An expression of the amount of solute mixed with a solvent.
A graph of reactant or product concentration as a function of time.
The conversion of a gas into a liquid.
A polymerization reaction between an acid and either an alcohol or an amine.
Any substance that has a proton that may be donated to a base.
A pair of substances whose formulas differ by one H+ ion.
A series of two or more double bonds, each separated by only a single bond in a molecule.
A graph showing the changes that occur while a substance is cooling.
The covalent bond between two atoms that is formed when one substance donates both electrons.
The equation that defines attractive and repulsive forces between charged particles.
The bond between two atoms that arises from the sharing of a pair of electrons.
A chemical compound in which the atoms are held together with covalent bonds.
A crystal that consists of only one molecule. All atoms are joined to others with covalent bonds. Also called network crystal.
The minimum mass of a fissile (fissionable) material needed to sustain a nuclear chain reaction.
The temperature and pressure above which a gas cannot be condensed to a liquid.
The arrangement of atoms, ions, or molecules in a crystal structure.
A machine for accelerating charged particles, which are usually used to bombard targets in an effort to generate nuclear reactions.
An orbital formed from one s, three p, and two d orbitals. The electrons in the hybrid all have the same energy. Structures are all related to the octahedron.
The law that the total pressure of a gas is the sum of the individual pressures of all the gases in the mixture; Ptotal = P1 + P2 + ...
The spontaneous emission of a particle in a radioactive event.
The variable that an experiment measures; its value depends on the value of the independent variable.
A molecular structure that is derived from one of the five basic structures.
A chemical substance that has both polar and nonpolar properties and is soluble in both polar and nonpolar solvents.
An error associated with faulty instruments, calibrations, or techniques.
A term describing an optical isomer that rotates polarized light to the right.
A term indicating that two elements in periods 2A and 3A and two groups, x and x + 1, respectively, have similar properties; for example, Li and Mg or B and Si.

A term describing the fact that some properties of atoms vary regularly from the lower left corner to the upper right corner of the periodic table. Electronegativity, ionization energy, and electron affinity are some of these diagonal relationships.
An allotrope of carbon in which all carbon atoms have sp3 hybridization.
A term describing a molecule that contains only two atoms (e.g., HCl, H2).
The electron that differentiates one element from an adjacent element in the periodic table.
The combination of light waves that results in either constructive or destructive reinforcement.
The movement of molecules from one place to another by random motion.
A qualitative term indicating a small amount of solute in a given amount of solvent.
A substance composed of two identical molecular or ionic units.
A polar molecule. The term dipole reminds us that a polar molecule has only two poles, one positive and one negative.
A relationship between two variables whereby one must increase when the other increases.
The breakup of an ionic compound into ions.
A chemical equation in which the cation of one substance replaces the cation of a second substance. At the same time, the cation of the second substance replaces the cation of the first substance.
An orbital formed from one s, three p, and one d orbital. The electrons in these orbitals are all equal in energy. Structures are all related to the trigonal bipyramid.
A term describing the property of being able to be drawn into wire forms.

The state in which a chemical process is going in the forward direction at the same rate that it is going in the reverse direction and the concentrations of reactants and products remain constant. Equilibrium follows the kinetic period, in which reaction occurs and the concentrations of reactants and products change.
Ethylenediamine tetraacetic acid, a very useful complexing agent.
The movement of molecules through a small hole from one container to another.
A metal placed in a liquid to transfer electrons in a galvanic or electrolytic cell.
The process of using electric current to reduce a chemical substance at the cathode and oxidize a chemical substance at the anode.
A substance that dissociates or ionizes completely into ions in solution.
An arrangement of electrodes and a power source used to force nonspontaneous redox reactions to occur.

1. The unit of negative charge in the atom. The diffuse electron cloud surrounds the dense nucleus.
2. One of the three particles, along with the proton and neutron, that make up an atom. An electron has a negative charge and virtually no mass in comparison to the neutron and proton. Electrons are arranged in an orderly fashion around the nucleus in a diffuse electron cloud. There are as many electrons as protons in an element.
The energy released or absorbed in adding an electron to an atom.
A term describing a Lewis structure that has fewer than an octet of electrons around one or more of its atoms, except hydrogen.
A measure of an atom's tendency to attract electrons. Fluorine has the highest, and francium the lowest, electronegativity in the periodic table.
A statement of the fact that no chemical compound has a net charge. In addition, an element has no net charge.

A listing of the electrons within an atom, based on the sublevels that are filled and the relative energies of these sublevels. For example, the electronic configuration for silicon is 1s22s22p63s23p2.
The energy of attraction of two oppositely charged particles, or the energy of repulsion of two like-charged particles.
Any one of the 117 distinct particles, known as atoms, that are currently known. Each has distinct chemical and physical properties.
One reaction in a mechanism. It is usually bimolecular or unimolecular, and its coefficients are the exponents in the rate law.
The formula that gives only the simplest whole-number ratio of the atoms that make up a compound. See also molecular formula; structural formula.
The point, where neither reactant is in excess, that marks the end of a titration experiment.
A term describing any process that absorbs heat from the surroundings. Endothermic processes cool the system.
The heat content of a chemical substance. Enthalpy is related to the internal potential energy of the substance.
Entropy of a system is proportional to the number of microstates in that system. This is a more precise definition than the randomness of a chemical system.
One of many naturally occurring catalysts found in biological materials.
The activated complex formed in an enzyme-catalyzed reaction.

A term used to describe the position of an atom in a covalent molecule of the AX5 or AX6 basic structure. The equatorial atoms are around the center of the molecule in positions similar to Earth's equator.
The numerical value of the equilibrium expression. The only variable that has an effect on the equilibrium constant is temperature.
The basic equation governing chemical equilibrium. Each balanced chemical equation has its own equilibrium expression.
A table of data used to summarize the numerical data and stoi­ chiometric relationships of an equilibrium system.
A value that is determined for a substance by dividing its mass by the equivalent weight.
The mass of a compound that loses or gains 1 mole of electrons in an oxidation-reduction reaction. In acid-base reactions it is the mass that furnishes or reacts with 1 mole of H+ ions.
The minimum kinetic energy of a liquid molecule that is needed for transformation into a gas.
An organic compound containing the -C-O-C- functional group.
A closed-end manometer.
The transformation of a liquid into a gas at a temperature below the boiling point.
A number that has no uncertainty. Exact numbers include stoichiometric coefficients, formula subscripts, and most defined quantities.
Any reactant that is not completely consumed in a chemical reaction.
A term describing any process that gives off heat to the surroundings. Exothermic processes heat the system.
A physical or chemical property that varies in proportion to the amount of matter.
A cubic structure in which atoms are at the corners and an atom is on each cube face of the unit cell.
A ratio used to convert a number with one set of units into the equivalent number with different units.
The relationship between the coulomb and moles of electrons; 96,485 C = 1 mol e−.
The liquid that passes through a filter.
The law that states that in any chemical or physical process all energy is conserved.
A reaction with a rate law having exponents that add up to 1. The rate law is Rate = k[A].
A term describing a nucleus that is capable of undergoing nuclear fission.

A property of some atoms and molecules that allows them to absorb photons of light and reemit them very rapidly but with a different energy. The emitted light always has a lower energy and longer wavelength than the absorbed light.
The charge on an atom in a covalent compound, calculated by assuring that all bonding electrons are equally shared.
A chemical reaction in which the reactants are elements at standard state and the product is 1 mole of one compound.
The representation of a chemical substance using chemical symbols and appropriate subscripts for the numbers of atoms and superscripts to represent charges if the substance is an ion.
A molecule that contains an unpaired electron in its Lewis structure.
The temperature decrease in the freezing point per molal °C m-1 of solute particles.
A group of atoms on an organic compound that represent a characteristic chemical entity.
The experimental setup used to convert chemical energy into electric energy. All batteries are galvanic cells.
A high-energy photon often emitted in a nuclear reaction.
A state of matter characterized by the ability to flow and fill any container completely without regard to the amount of gas in the container.
The law that expresses the direct relationship between the temperature and pressure of a gas; P/T = constant.
The maximum energy from any chemical reaction.
The law that relates the rate at which gases pass through a small hole to the mass of the molecule; `sqrt(m_1//m_2)=bar(v_2)//bar(v_1)`.
A pictorial method of presenting and evaluating experimental data.
An allotrope of carbon in which carbon has sp2 hybridization.
The attractive energy of any two masses toward each other.
A column in the periodic table.
The time required for half of the reactants to be consumed in a first-order chemical reaction or a radioactive decay.
An organic compound with a halogen (e.g., CH3, CH2, Cl) in its structure.
An element in the next to last group of the periodic table. Halogens are reactive elements with ns2 , np5 valence electron structures.
The addition of a halogen to a double or triple bond.
The amount of heat energy that a system needs in order for its temperature to change by 1 °C.
The heat released when 1 mole of sample, usually an organic compound, is completely burned in oxygen to form CO2 and H2O.
The heat energy needed to convert a solid into a liquid. The units are either joules per gram or joules per mole.
The heat energy needed to convert a liquid into a gas. The units are either joules per gram or joules per mole.
A graph showing the changes that occur while a substance is heated.
A derivation of the equilibrium expression obtained by taking the negative logarithm of the equilibrium expression; pH = pKa + log([conjugate base]/[conjugate acid]).
The law that expresses the relationship between the solubility of a gas and its partial pressure; c = kp.
The law that states that heats of reaction are additive when chemical reactions are added.
The rule that every orbital in a sublevel must fill with one electron before a second electron of opposite spin can be added to any orbital in that sublevel.

An orbital constructed by combining electrons, usually from s and p orbitals, into a new orbital where all the electrons have the same properties. These orbitals are designated as sp, sp2, sp3, dsp3, and d2sp3.

A substance that contains a fixed number of water molecules. The water molecules are written separately from the formula itself and connected to it with a dot in the center of the line between the chemical formula and the water molecules (e.g., CuSO4·5 H2O).
An extra-strength dipole-dipole attractive force due to a large electronegativity difference between hydrogen and nitrogen, oxygen, or fluorine.
The addition of H2 to a double or triple bond.
The addition of a hydrogen and a halogen to a double or triple bond by using a binary acid such as HF, HCl, HBr, or HI.
The reaction of a substance, usually a conjugate acid or base, with water.
A gas that obeys the ideal gas law; conceptually, a gas molecule with no volume and no attractive forces with other molecules.
The law that relates temperature, pressure, volume, and moles of gas; PV = nRT.
The variable in an experiment that is under the control of the experimenter.
An error in estimating the uncertain digit in a measurement. Also called random error.
A chemical added to a titration experiment that changes color at the end point.
An electrode placed in a sample in order to measure the concentration of an ion in the sample.
A dipole formed by the interaction of a nonpolar substance and either a polar substance or an instantaneous dipole.
A quantitative description of a chemical system at the start of a reaction.

A method for balancing chemical equations. The inspection involves counting the number of each atom present in the equation and then balancing by adding appropriate coefficients to the reactants or products.
A distortion of the electron cloud around an atom or molecule that gives the atom or molecule momentary polarity.
A substance that appears in the elementary reactions of a mechanism but not in the overall balanced equation.
The attractive forces-dipole-dipole attractions, London forces, and hydrogen bonding-between molecules and atoms that allow them to condense into liquids and solidify into solids.
An imaginary line connecting the nuclei of two atoms.
A physical or chemical property that does not change with the amount of matter.
A relationship between two variables whereby one must increase if the other decreases.
An element that has lost or gained one or more electrons. See also polyatomic ion.
A method for balancing more complex oxidation-reduction equations. It involves a logical sequence of steps.
The attraction of a negative anion for a positive cation.
A chemical compound composed of negatively charged anions and positively charged cations. The unit is held together by the attraction of the positive charges toward the negative charges.
A crystal formed from cations and anions where the main attractive force is the attraction of positive charges toward negative charges.
The removal or addition of an electron from an atom or molecule. Also the formation of ions when a molecular substance dissolves in water.
The energy required to remove an electron completely from an atom.
A term describing any two atoms that have identical electronic configurations. These atoms may be ions or elements.
A system in which neither mass nor energy is transferred to or from the surroundings.
Distinctly different compounds that have the same elemental composition.
A form of an element with a specified number of protons, neutrons, and electrons.
International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry, which sets nomenclature standards.
The symbol for the equilibrium constant, often written as Keq.
The acid dissociation constant, a special term denoting the equilibrium of a weak acid. A weak acid dissociation is always in the form `HA+text(H)_2text(O)harrtext(A)^(-)+text(H)_3text(O)^(+)`
The base dissociation constant, a special term denoting the equilibrium of a weak base. A weak base dissociation is always in the form `text(B)+text(H)_2text(O)harrBH^(+)+OH^(-)`
The equilibrium constant used when the reactants and products are specified as concentrations.
The dissociation constant, a special term used mainly to describe the dissociation of complex ions.
An organic compound with a nonterminal -C=O group.
The formation constant, a special term used to describe the formation of complex ions.
A graph of reactant or product concentration as a function of time.
The energy that matter possesses because of its motion; `KE=1/2mv^2`.
The theory of the motion of molecules in the gas phase, which explains gas pressure, effusion and diffusion rates, and the effect of temperature on the behavior of gases.
The equilibrium constant used when the reactants and products are specified in terms of partial pressures.
The solubility product, a special term denoting the fact that the equilibrium is between a solid and its solution products.
The autopyrolysis constant of water, equal to 1.0 × 10-14 at 25 °C.
An expression of the fact that the strongest acid in water is the H+ (H3O+) ion and the strongest base is the hydroxide ion, OH−.
A term describing an optical isomer that rotates polarized light to the left.
Any substance that can accept electron pairs.
Any substance that can donate electron pairs. Also called ligand; complexing agent; sequestering agent.
A molecular structure based on the concept that all atoms try to achieve the noble gas electronic configuration by sharing electrons.
The theory that acids are electron-pair acceptors and bases are electron-pair donors.
The reactant that is completely consumed in a reaction, causing it to stop. Also called limiting reagent.
A term referring to atoms aligned in a straight line; a three-atom arrangement with a 180° bond angle.
A state of matter characterized by its ability to flow in order to fill any container from the bottom up.
A type of pH paper using the indicator litmus, which is pink in acid and blue in base.
The analogy used to depict how an enzyme recognizes reactants on the basis of physical geometry as well as chemical characteristics.

The attractive forces from instantaneous dipoles. These forces are due to the possibility that the electron clouds around atoms and molecules are not perfectly symmetrical at all times. Also called dispersion forces.
Electron pairs in Lewis structures that are not used for bonding.
The quantum number that specifies the orbital in which an electron is located and the orientation of the orbital in space; mℓ may be any number from -1 to +1, including zero.
A term describing the property of being able to be hammered into new shapes.
A device used for measuring gas pressures.
A quantity of matter.
A concentration unit defined as the mass of one solute divided by the total mass of the solution.
A concentration unit defined as the mass of one solute in a given total volume of solution.
The temperature at which a solid melts at 1.00 atmo­ sphere of pressure; also, the temperature at which a liquid becomes a solid. Also called crystallization point.
The curved surface of a liquid in a tube or container.
A substance with characteristic properties of high electrical conductivity, malleability, and a metallic silver or yellow luster.
A crystal formed from a metal in the periodic table. Metallic crystals are malleable and ductile and conduct electricity.
An element that has properties of both metals and nonmetals.
A term describing a physical situation in which a material is stable unless disturbed.
One of seven basic units of measurement in the metric system. More complex units are combinations of base units.
A prefix (e.g., milli-, pico-) used with a metric base unit to represent a specific exponential value.
A description of stereoisomers in which the structure of one isomer is the reflection of the other in a mirror.
A concentration unit defined as the number of moles of solute dissolved in 1 kilogram of solvent.
The sum of the gram-atomic masses of all atoms in a chemical formula. Also called molecular mass.
The volume of 1 mole of gas, usually at standard temperature and pressure (STP).
A concentration unit defined as the number of moles of solute in 1 liter of solution.
The quantity of any substance that contains 6.02 × 1023 units of that substance.
A concentration unit defined as the number of moles of solute divided by the total number of moles in a solution.
A crystal formed from a molecule. The attractive forces that hold molecular crystals together are London forces, dipole-dipole attractions, hydrogen bonding, or a combination of these.

The formula for a molecular or covalent substance, showing all of the atoms that comprise the molecular unit. A molecular formula may be simplified to an empirical formula if all of the subscripts can be divided by a common number. See also empirical formula; structural formula.
An orbital created by the pairing of electrons from different atoms. This orbital encircles the atoms that are bonded together.
A group of atoms bound together by covalent bonds with zero total charge.
A solid salt that has been heated to a temperature where it becomes a liquid. Also called a fused salt.
A term describing light that has a single wavelength.
A Lewis base that donates one pair of electrons.
One of the individual repeating units of a polymer.
The percentage of an isotope of an element found in nature.
A chemical reaction of an acid with a base.

One of three particles, along with the electron and proton, that make up an atom. This particle has no charge but has a mass approximately equal to the proton mass. Neutrons and protons make up the bulk of the mass of the atom.
An element in the last group in the periodic table. Noble gases are unusually stable elements and all have ns2, np6 valence electrons.
A pair of electrons in a Lewis structure that is not shared with any other atoms.
A substance that does not dissociate at all in solution.
An element that is not metallic. Nonmetals do not conduct electricity well and do not have a shiny metallic luster. They are located in the upper right portion of the periodic table.
A term describing a bond or molecule that has its charge distributed evenly. Only diatomic elements form truly nonpolar bonds. Symmetrical molecules are nonpolar.
A term describing an organic compound in which all carbon atoms are arranged in one straight chain.
The number of equivalents of a substance dissolved in 1 liter of solution.
The number of positive charges in the nucleus. This is the same as the number of protons in the nucleus (Z) and is also the atomic number.
A radioactive decay process initiated by the absorption of a neutron; it results in a large nucleus dividing roughly in half.
The combination of two nuclei to form a new atom.
The total mass of the nucleus. This is the sum of the masses of the protons and neutrons in the nucleus. Since electrons have virtually no mass, it is also the atomic mass (A) of the isotope.
A device that uses a nuclear reaction to create heat energy for the purpose of generating electricity.
Either a proton or a neutron, both of which are fundamental particles of the nucleus.
The center of an atom, which contains the protons and neutrons. The nucleus is extremely dense and comprises a very small fraction of the atom's volume; the rest of the atom is empty space.
A geometric structure of six atoms covalently bound to a central atom. Each atom is 90° from any other.

A simple but effective rule stating that covalent molecules tend to have octets of electrons around each atom in their structures. These octets simulate the electron configurations of the noble gases.
A system in which matter and energy can be exchanged with the surroundings.
A stereoisomer that rotates polarized light.
The thickness of a sample in a spectroscopic experiment.

A region of space that may be occupied by a maximum of two electrons. The shape of an orbital is defined by the sublevel it is in. The orientation of the orbital depends on its assigned quantum number, mℓ. Every orbital in a given sublevel must be filled with one electron before a second electron may fill the orbital.
A diagram in which boxes represent individual valence orbitals. Electrons are represented as arrows to show the spins of the electrons in each orbital.
The sum of the exponents in a rate law.
An acid containing carbon and the -COOH functional group.
A compound composed of carbon and usually hydrogen.
The pressure needed to stop the migration of solute through a semipermeable membrane.
The loss of electrons; also, the increase in oxidation number.
A substance that causes another to be oxidized; also, a substance that itself is reduced. This term is commonly used by chemists, but it is not on the AP exam.
The pressure of a single gas in a mixture of gases.
A unit of measurement similar in concept to percent, obtained by multiplying a fraction by one billion (109).
A unit of measurement similar in concept to percent, obtained by multiplying a fraction by one million (106).
The requirement that no two electrons in an atom have the same set of four quantum numbers, n, l, ml, and ms.
A unit of measurement meaning parts per hundred, obtained by multiplying a fraction by 100.
A row in the periodic table.
The table in which the elements are arranged in an orderly fashion that shows the relationships of their chemical and physical characteristics.
The negative logarithm of the hydrogen ion concentration in a solution; pH = -log H+.
A weak acid or a weak base whose conjugate acid and conjugate base have different colors. An indicator changes color indicating the end point of a titration.
An electronic device used to measure the pH values of solutions.
Paper with a pH indicator absorbed on it so that it changes color ­ depending on the pH of the solution; pH paper is used to estimate pH. See also litmus paper.
A graph showing the relationship between temperature and pressure and the conversion of matter among three states: solid, liquid, and gas.

A property of some atoms and molecules that allows them to absorb photons of light and reemit them seconds to hours later. The emitted light always has a lower energy and therefore a longer wavelength than the absorbed light.
A bond made from the sideways overlap of two p orbitals. The electron density of a pi bond lies outside the internuclear axis.
A narrow tube calibrated for precise measurement of small volumes of liquids.
The negative logarithm of the autopyrolysis constant of water, equal to 14.00.
A geometric structure of four atoms, three bonded to a central atom with 120° angles between the atoms, which are all in the same plane.
The constant relating the energy of a photon to its frequency.
An experimental setup for collecting gases by the displacement of water.
The negative logarithm of the hydroxide ion concentration in a solution; pOH= - log OH−.
A term describing the property of a covalent bond or molecule of having one end more positive than the other.
The tendency for an atom's electron cloud to be deformed so that polarity is created.
An ion composed of more than one atom covalently bonded together. A polyatomic ion acts as a unit in most chemical reactions.
An acid with two or more ionizable hydrogen atoms in its formula.
A positive electron.
The energy of matter that may, under appropriate conditions, be converted into work.

1. (v.) To cause the formation of a solid by a chemical reaction.
2. (n.) The solid formed as a result of a chemical reaction.
The degree of closeness of a group of repeated measurements to each other.
The force per unit area; gas molecules exert this force by collisions with the container walls.
The quantum number that specifies the energy level of the atom in which an electron is located; n may be any integer from 1 to infinity.
The result of a chemical reaction. Products are placed on the right-hand side of a chemical equation.

One of three particles, along with the electron and neutron, that make up an atom. The proton has a positive charge, equal in magnitude (but with the opposite sign) to the charge of the electron. The number of protons is equal to the atomic number, Z, of an element. Protons and neutrons make up the bulk of the mass of an atom.
A term referring to a description of a physical or chemical property without the use of numbers or equations.
A logical sequence of experiments and observations used to determine the composition of a sample.
A term referring to a description of a physical or chemical property using numbers or equations.
One of four numbers (n, ℓ, mℓ, ms) used in the wave-mechanical model of the atom to describe an electron in an atom.
An equal molar mixture of L and D optical isomers.
A sequence of radioactive disintegrations from a heavy isotope to a lighter, stable isotope in more than one step.
The property that some unstable nuclei have of decaying spontaneously with the emission of a small particle and/or energy.
A radioactive isotope of an element.
A qualitative description of the disorder of the molecules in any sample.
The law that expresses the relationship between the vapor pressure of a solution and the mole fraction of solute in that solution.
A constant in the direct relationship between the amount of reacting substance and the rate of the reaction.
The mathematical relationship between reactant concentrations and reaction rate. The general form of a rate law is Rate = k[A]x[B]y[C]z
The slowest reaction in a mechanism, which limits the overall rate of reaction. Also called rate-limiting step.
One of the starting materials in a chemical reaction. The reactants are placed on the left side of a chemical equation.
The detailed series of elementary reactions that add up to the overall reaction. See also elementary reaction.
A plot of the potential energy of molecules as they collide in a reaction, illustrating the nature of the activation energy.
The value of the ratio of the equilibrium expression when a chemi­ cal system is not in a state of equilibrium. The value of Q in comparison to that of K indicates the direction of the reaction.
The velocity, in moles per liter per second, at which reactants are converted into products in a chemical reaction.
A solution used to set the zero point of a spectrophotometer.
A gas in which there are attractive forces between the molecules and the molecules have a finite volume.
A word coined to combine the terms reduction and oxidation. It indicates that reduction and oxidation always occur together.
A substance that causes another substance to be reduced; also, a substance that is oxidized. This term is commonly used by chemists, but it is not on the AP exam.
The gain of electrons; also, the decrease in oxidation number.
An electrode in a galvanic cell, which has a constant potential since the concentrations of all reactants are kept constant.
A term describing the fact that the masses of atoms in the periodic table are relative, without units, as compared to the mass of the carbon-12 isotope.
The absolute uncertainty of a measurement divided by the value of the measurement.
A Lewis structure that can be drawn in more than one equally probable way. The actual structure is a mixture of all possible resonance structures.
A chemical or physical process that can be changed from one state to another and then back to the original state. A reversible process takes place in infinitesimally small steps.
The standard entropy of 1 mole of a substance.
A term describing an organic compound in which all carbon-carbon bonds are single bonds. Saturated compounds have the maximum number of hydrogen atoms; that is, they are saturated with hydrogen.
A solution that has the maximum amount of solute dissolved in it.

A method of writing numbers in which the significant figures are numbers greater than or equal to 1 and less than 10, and they are multiplied by 10 raised to the appropriate power to indicate the position of the decimal point.
The law that states that in all physical and chemical processes the overall entropy of the universe must increase.
A reaction with a rate law having exponents that add up to 2. The rate law is Rate = k[A][B] or Rate = [A]2.
A thin, solid material through which certain molecules can diffuse while others cannot; may be visualized as a barrier with small holes that allow only molecules of a certain size to pass through.

The old term for the principal energy level of an electron; the region in space where electrons are located around the nucleus of the atom. Energy levels are numbered starting with the energy level closest to the nucleus. The number of the principal energy level is also known as the principal quantum number.
A covalent bond formed by the sharing of a pair of electrons. The electron pair is located along the internuclear axis between the two atoms that share it.
All the digits in a measurement except preceding zeros.
A term describing a cubic structure with one atom in each of the eight corners of a unit cell.
A state of matter characterized by a rigid structure that retains its shape without a container.
A property of a solute that refers to the maximum amount of that solute that can be dissolved in a solvent. This term can be a qualitative or quantitative description of a solute.
The substance-gas, liquid, or solid-dissolved in the solvent.
A uniform mixture of chemicals. In a solution it is impossible to distinguish separate solute and solvent particles.
Typically, the liquid phase in which a gas, another liquid, or a solid is dissolved. In a mixture of two or more liquids the solvent is the liquid present in the largest amount.
An orbital constructed from an s and a p orbital into one where both have equal energies. The resulting structures related to this orbital are linear.
An orbital constructed from an s and two p orbitals. The resulting orbitals all have the same energy. Structures related to this orbital are trigonal planar.
An orbital constructed from an s and three p orbitals. The resulting orbitals all have the same energy. Structures related to this orbital are tetrahedral.
An intrinsic property of matter that describes the quantity of heat energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 gram of substance by 1 °C.
An instrument for determining the amount of light absorbed by a sample.
The quantum number that specifies the spin of an electron as either `+1/2` or `-1/2`. Two electrons in the same orbital must have opposite spins.
The voltage of a galvanic cell when the system is at standard state; also, the combination of two standard reduction potentials as E°cell = E°cathode - E°anode.
The potential (voltage) of a reduction half-reaction at standard state.

Defined temperature, pressure, and concentrations. In electrochemistry the standard state is 1.00 atmosphere pressure, 298 K or 25 °C, and 1.00 molar concentrations for all soluble compounds. Solids and pure liquids are also defined as 1.00 molar.
A state defined as having a temperature of 0 °C and 1 atmosphere of pressure.
A variable whose value depends only on the initial and final states of the system. State functions are ∆H, ∆S, ∆G, and ∆E.

The assumption that, in evaluating rate constants for elementary reactions, the concentrations of intermediates may be mathematically eliminated by assuming that all prior fast steps are in chemical equilibrium.
Compounds that have the same formula and same bonding but differ in the geometric arrangement of the atoms.
A term describing a chemical reaction that produces only one stereoisomer.
Mathematical relationships between chemical substances in a chemical equation.
The valve on the end of a buret.
An acid that dissociates completely when dissolved in water.
A base that dissociates completely when dissolved in water.
A formula that shows the actual arrangement of atoms within the molecule and the bonds between the atoms. See also empirical formula; molecular formula.
Compounds with the same formula but with the atoms bonded in different arrangements.

A subdivision of an energy level. Electrons in each principal energy level are localized in sublevels. Each sublevel has a distinct shape associated with it. Sublevels are numbered from zero up to one less than the number of the principal energy level. These sublevel numbers are the azimuthal quantum numbers, ℓ. Sublevels are also designated by the letters s, p, d, f.
A number placed to the right of, and slightly below, the symbol for an element to represent the number of times that atom is present in the formula unit.
The reactant(s) in an enzyme-catalyzed reaction.
The property of some materials capable of being cooled to temperatures below their melting points without solidifying. Supercooled solutions are also supersaturated and are metastable.
A gas at a temperature and pressure above the critical point. Such a fluid has properties of both a gas and a liquid.
The liquid remaining above a solid after centrifugation.
A metastable solution that has more than the maximum amount of solute dissolved in it.
The added attractive force per molecule at the surface of a liquid. Surface tension causes liquids to assume shapes that minimize surface area.
A substance that lowers the surface tension of liquids.
All parts of the universe not included in the system being studied.
A term describing a geometrical property whereby a structure may be rotated by some angle less than 360° and after rotation the molecule has the same configuration as before.
The portion of the universe that is under study.
A label on glassware indicating that the item is calibrated to contain the indicated volume.
A label on glassware indicating that the calibration is based on the volume delivered.
The addition polymer of CF2=CF2 with extraordinary nonstick properties.
A geometric structure with four atoms bound to a central atom by covalent bonds. Each bond is equidistant from any other with a bond angle of 109°.
Any reaction that occurs without outside assistance; quantitatively, any reaction that has an equilibrium constant greater than 1.
The study of energy changes in chemical and physical processes.
An experimental procedure for reacting two solutions in order to determine the quantity or concentration of one of the solutions.
A plot of pH versus the volume of titrant added to a sample.
A radioactive element used to detect the movement of materials in a complex system.
An isomer with substituents on opposite sides of a double bond.
An element having a d electron as the differentiating electron in its electronic configuration.
The reaction-rate theory that details the events and energy changes that occur as two molecules collide.
Any of the 17 elements from atomic number 93 to 109.

A geometric structure with five atoms covalently bound to a central atom. Three atoms in the equatorial position are 120° from each other. Two additional atoms in the axial positions are 90° from the equatorial atoms.
The temperature and pressure at which all three states of matter-solid, liquid, and gas-are in equilibrium.
The fundamental building block of crystals. An entire crystal is formed by repetitive stacking of the unit cells.
The constant needed to relate the temperature, pressure, volume, and moles of gas in the ideal gas law, PV = nRT.
The entirety of all matter and space that exist.
A term describing an organic compound that contains one or more double or triple bonds in its structure.
A solution in which the solute concentration is less than the maximum amount possible.
The laboratory technique of vaporizing and condensing a liquid for the purpose of purification. Vacuum distillation is used to reduce the boiling points of heat-sensitive compounds.
The outermost s and p electrons in an atom. The number and the arrangement of valence electrons define chemical and physical properties.
A method of evaluating molecular structure by relating the number of bonding and nonbonding electron pairs on an atom to its geometrical structure.
The pressure developed by a liquid or solid in a closed container at a constant temperature.
The ability of a fluid to flow. The more easily a fluid flows, the lower is its viscosity.
A concentration unit defined as the volume of one liquid solute divided by the total volumes of the liquids mixed to prepare a solution.
A flask calibrated to contain a precise volume of liquid.
An acid that dissociates slightly when dissolved in water.
A substance that partially dissociates into ions in solution.
The force developed by the gravitational attraction of two masses.
An average that depends on the abundance of the objects being averaged.
The spreading of a liquid on a surface that occurs because the adhesive forces overcome the cohesive forces in the liquid.
The high-energy electromagnetic radiation emitted in nuclear decay events or when certain metals are bombarded with energetic electrons.
A reaction in which the rate is independent of reactant concentration. The rate law is Rate = k.
The energy change due to a chemical reaction. It is equal to the heat and work of the reaction or to the change in potential energy of the products as compared to that of the reactants.
The standard free-energy change for a reaction. The temperature is 298 K unless otherwise indicated.
The standard free-energy change of formation corresponding to the formation of 1 mole of product from its elements at 298 K.
The enthalpy change occurring in a chemical process. Without the superscript zero it indicates an extensive property. Often called the heat of reaction.
The standard enthalpy change occurring in a reaction; refers to the heat produced or absorbed when the moles of reactants specified in the chemical reaction react at standard state.
The standard heat of formation, which is the heat produced or absorbed when 1 mole of a product is formed.
The change in entropy between the final state and the initial state in a chemical process. Without the superscript zero it indicates an extensive property.
The standard entropy change of a chemical process; an intensive property based on the moles of substance in the balanced chemical reaction.
